draft.title: The logistic equation
card: The logistic equation models a population P that grows quickly at first, then slows as it nears a limit. The limit is the carrying capacity, N, the largest population the environment can support.
The equation is dP/dt = kP(1 − P/N), where k > 0 and N > 0. The factor (1 − P/N) is close to 1 when P is small and close to 0 when P is near N.
If 0 < P < N, then dP/dt > 0 and the population rises towards N. If P > N, then dP/dt < 0 and it falls towards N. If P = N or P = 0, then dP/dt = 0 and the population does not change.
Example: dP/dt = 0.2P(1 − P/500). When P = 100, dP/dt = 0.2 × 100 × (1 − 0.2) = 16. The population is growing at 16 per unit of time.
draft.remember: Logistic growth is fastest when P is small, then slows to zero rate as P reaches N.

a.q: A population follows dP/dt = 0.3P(1 − P/800). What is the carrying capacity?
a.why: The equation has the form dP/dt = kP(1 − P/N), so N = 800. The number 0.3 is the growth constant k, which is not a population limit.
a.clue: Match the equation to the form with N inside the bracket.

b.q: A pond population follows dP/dt = 0.1P(1 − P/200). At P = 100, what is dP/dt?
b.why: dP/dt = 0.1 × 100 × (1 − 100/200) = 10 × 0.5 = 5. The value 10 comes from forgetting the bracket, and 2.5 comes from halving the bracket twice.
b.clue: Work out the bracket first, then multiply by 0.1P.

problems.detail: Logistic growth is not fastest when P is small. dP/dt = kP(1 − P/N) is largest at P = N/2. When P is small the rate is close to 0 (only the relative rate, the factor (1 − P/N), is near its largest). The line teaches a wrong idea about the S-shaped curve.

'Grows quickly at first' is misleading. From a small starting population, logistic growth starts slowly, speeds up until P = N/2, then slows as P nears N. The card should say the rate is greatest at P = N/2, or say plainly that the relative growth rate is what is largest at first.

check.summary: Both questions and their answers are correct. The remember line wrongly says logistic growth is fastest when P is small (it is fastest at P = N/2), and the card's 'grows quickly at first' backs up the same misconception.

final.title: The logistic equation
card: The logistic equation models a population \(P\) with a limit \(N\), the carrying capacity: the largest population the environment can support. From a small start, \(P\) grows slowly, speeds up until \(P = \frac{N}{2}\), then slows as it nears \(N\).

The equation is \(\frac{dP}{dt} = kP\left(1 - \frac{P}{N}\right)\), where \(k > 0\) and \(N > 0\). The factor \(\left(1 - \frac{P}{N}\right)\) is close to 1 when \(P\) is small and close to 0 when \(P\) is near \(N\).

If \(0 < P < N\), then \(\frac{dP}{dt} > 0\) and the population rises towards \(N\). If \(P > N\), then \(\frac{dP}{dt} < 0\) and it falls towards \(N\). If \(P = N\) or \(P = 0\), then \(\frac{dP}{dt} = 0\) and the population does not change.

Example: \(\frac{dP}{dt} = 0.2P\left(1 - \frac{P}{500}\right)\). When \(P = 100\), \(\frac{dP}{dt} = 0.2 \times 100 \times \left(1 - \frac{100}{500}\right)\), which is \(20 \times 0.8 = 16\). The population is growing at 16 per unit of time.

1.alt: A logistic curve, \(P = \frac{500}{1 + 24e^{-0.2t}}\), for a population with carrying capacity \(N = 500\), shown as a dashed line. From a small start the population grows slowly, then fastest at \(P = \frac{N}{2}\) (250), then more slowly as it nears \(N\).

final.remember: The rate \(kP\left(1 - \frac{P}{N}\right)\) peaks at \(P = \frac{N}{2}\) and falls to 0 as \(P\) reaches \(N\).

a.q: A population follows \(\frac{dP}{dt} = 0.3P\left(1 - \frac{P}{800}\right)\). What is the carrying capacity?
a.why: The equation has the form \(\frac{dP}{dt} = kP\left(1 - \frac{P}{N}\right)\), so \(N = 800\). The number 0.3 is the growth constant \(k\), not a population limit, and 400 is \(\frac{N}{2}\), where growth is fastest.
a.clue: Match the equation to the form with \(N\) inside the bracket.

b.q: A pond population follows \(\frac{dP}{dt} = 0.1P\left(1 - \frac{P}{200}\right)\). At \(P = 100\), what is \(\frac{dP}{dt}\)?
b.why: \(\frac{dP}{dt} = 0.1 \times 100 \times \left(1 - \frac{100}{200}\right)\), which is \(10 \times 0.5 = 5\). The value 10 comes from leaving out the bracket. The value 0 mixes up the point where the rate is largest, \(P = \frac{N}{2}\), with a rate of zero.
b.clue: Work out the bracket first, then multiply by \(0.1P\).
